item.title: Why Recognizing Limerence Is Not the Same as Pathologizing Love
item.description:
Limerence

Why Recognizing Limerence Is Not the Same as Pathologizing Love

Love isn't pathological. Debilitating, intrusive obsession is.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Limerence is not love, but a distinct, disruptive state marked by obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours
  • Recognizing limerence as clinically significant does not mean pathologizing love or attraction.
  • Emotions exist on a spectrum; intensity alone doesn't distinguish normal experience from pathology.
  • The threshold for concern is persistence, intrusiveness, and disruption to daily functioning.
Source: Maya Alexa G Romero/Unsplash

I was recently interviewed for a New York Times article about limerence. As I read through the comments that followed, I noticed a striking divide. Many readers expressed relief at finally finding a word that described an experience they had struggled to understand, sometimes for years. Others reacted quite differently, arguing that psychology was once again attempting to pathologize a basic human emotion. To them, limerence was simply another name for being in love.

Both reactions are understandable.

For those who have experienced limerence, discovering that their intense and isolating experience has a name can be profoundly validating. For others, the suggestion that romantic longing could be viewed through a clinical lens raises concerns about the increasing tendency to medicalize ordinary human experience. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but they also reflect a common misunderstanding about what limerence is and what clinicians mean when they describe an experience as pathological.

No one is suggesting that love, attraction, longing, or romantic infatuation are mental disorders. These are universal aspects of human experience that enrich our lives, foster pair bonding, and have inspired some of humanity's greatest achievements in art, literature, and music (Fletcher et al., 2015). The question is not whether love can be intense. Rather, it is whether an experience that begins with attraction can, in some individuals, become so persistent, intrusive, and disruptive that it no longer resembles healthy romantic attachment.

Psychology has long recognized that normal emotional experiences exist on a continuum. Sadness is a healthy emotion, but when it becomes persistent and significantly impairs functioning, it may be recognized as Major Depressive Disorder. Anxiety serves an important evolutionary purpose, but excessive and uncontrollable anxiety may meet the criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Fear protects us from danger, yet irrational and debilitating fear may present as a specific phobia. In each of these cases, the emotion itself is not pathological. Rather, it is the intensity, persistence, and impact of the emotional state that distinguishes normal human experience from a mental health condition.

The same principle may reasonably apply to romantic attachment.

Limerence, first described by psychologist Dorothy Tennov (1979), is characterized by intrusive and obsessive thoughts about a specific person, emotional volatility, compulsive rumination, idealization, and an overwhelming desire for emotional reciprocation. While it may resemble the early stages of romantic love, it follows a markedly different trajectory. Healthy love typically develops into a secure attachment or gradually fades if the relationship cannot progress. Limerence does neither. Instead, it remains suspended in uncertainty, sustained by hope and doubt, while the individual becomes increasingly consumed by obsessive thoughts and emotional dependency.

Interestingly, the idea that limerence may have clinically significant pathological features is not new. Tennov herself described her work as a preliminary report that "only scratches the surface" and called for further research into the phenomenon (Tennov, 1979). Since then, several researchers have argued that limerence should be distinguished from normative romantic love. Wakin and Vo (2008) proposed that limerence shares characteristics with obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction, while Willmott and Bentley (2015) identified associations with anxiety, depression, trauma, and compulsive thinking. More recently, Bradbury et al. (2024) described limerence as a state of obsessive rumination and fixation, and Wyant (2021) proposed a cognitive behavioural framework for understanding and treating it.

The consequences of failing to recognize limerence extend beyond academic debate. In my clinical work, I have met numerous individuals who sought therapy specifically because they were experiencing limerence. Many described the relief of finally discovering a word that captured what they had been struggling with for months or even years. Others told me that when they sought professional help, their therapist had never heard of limerence and advised them to "just let go" or "focus on something else." While these suggestions are well intentioned, they are rarely helpful. Just as someone with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder cannot simply stop having intrusive thoughts, people experiencing limerence cannot simply decide to stop thinking about the person they are obsessing over. If they could, believe me, they would.

Some people worry that recognizing limerence as a potential mental health condition would contribute to the over-medicalization of ordinary human experience. This is a legitimate concern, and psychologists should always exercise caution before expanding the boundaries of psychopathology. However, the solution is not to dismiss genuine psychological suffering because it resembles a normal emotion. The solution is to maintain a clear threshold. Limerence is not defined by butterflies, infatuation, or the excitement of falling in love. It is characterized by persistent intrusive thoughts, emotional volatility, significant distress, and disruption to important areas of functioning. These are the features that warrant clinical attention.

Whether limerence is eventually recognized as a distinct mental health condition will ultimately be determined by further research. What should not be overlooked, however, is the reality of the suffering experienced by those living with it. Recognizing that severe romantic obsession may become psychologically impairing does not pathologize love any more than recognizing depression pathologizes sadness or recognizing Generalized Anxiety Disorder pathologizes worry. Rather, it acknowledges that human emotions exist on a spectrum and that, under certain circumstances, even our most adaptive emotions can become sources of profound distress. Greater awareness of limerence is therefore not about diminishing the richness of romantic love but ensuring that those whose lives have become consumed by obsessive longing are understood, supported, and offered appropriate care.

item.title: Your Mind Is Poison; Fortunately, It Is Also the Antidote
item.description:
Self-Sabotage

Your Mind Is Poison; Fortunately, It Is Also the Antidote

That which we attempt to suppress is exactly that which pops into our heads.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • It appears to be human nature to occasionally think and act against our best interests.
  • In this way, our minds can become a sort of poison that negatively impacts or lives.
  • Limiting this process involves thought acceptance rather than suppression.
Poison Bottle
Source: qimono / Pixabay

In 1845, Edgar Allen Poe wrote about a phenomenon that I see nearly every day in my clinical practice. In a short story of the same title, he wrote of The Imp of the Perverse. As his prose is far superior to mine, this is his understanding of it.

“Examine these and similar actions as we will, we shall find them resulting solely from the spirit of the Perverse. We perpetuate them merely because we feel that we should not.”

Poe was not a psychologist, but it is fair to say that he had a remarkable understanding of the human mind and human behavior, especially the darker forms of each. Nearly all his stories include psychological underpinnings that are just as relevant today.

One such concept is the Imp. How this manifests today is through self-sabotage and the tendency to think or act against our own self-interest. It is also the 3 a.m. anxiety attack telling us we will fail at something the next day. Our minds have the uncanny talent of finding the worst case scenario and making it seem plausible, if not likely. That is the poison. Not surprisingly, our bodies respond to the feared scenario by activating the sympathetic nervous system (flight or fight). Goodbye good night’s sleep. Goodbye self-confidence and inner peace. The poison has moved from our mind to our bodies.

A popular psychological study also supports this. Social psychologist Daniel Wegner encouraged subjects to not think of a white bear. Consistent with Poe’s Imp, they were more likely to think of the white bear. He called it ironic process theory, and it is relevant to many aspects of our life, including not thinking about cigarettes if we're trying to quit, as well as chronic pain or anxiety. That which we attempt to suppress is exactly that which pops into our heads.

Why do we do it? The most likely theory here is that the brain hates surprises and loves certainty. Our minds would rather be sure of a terrible outcome rather than wrestle with the unknown. Yes, even a plane crash is better than the unknown according to our survival-focused brains.

What is to be done? This is the tricky part—the antidote to the poison that our minds create. It is not always easy, but studies have found ways to successfully curb our biggest fears. Here is what I recommend to patients based on the findings:

  • Stop fighting your mind (you will lose). Instead, examine the unwanted, often terrifying thought. After all, it’s just a thought. If your mind is telling you that you will embarrass yourself during tomorrow’s big presentation, acknowledge it. Tell yourself, “Yes, I am struggling with anxiety and fear because the presentation is important to me.”
  • Next, gently challenge the thought. Tell yourself, “I’ve given presentations in the past and did pretty well.” Of course, your mind will offer another bit of poison by searching your mental database for the one time you dropped the ball. Again, don’t back down. Tell yourself that you are better prepared for this one (always a good practice anyway) and that you have grown as a presenter since then.
  • Turn anxiety into excitement. This is the main character energy. Perhaps you would prefer to hide rather than be a public speaker. Perhaps you would prefer to never fly again rather than face anxiety about it. That is the poison again. I work with professional athletes who thrive on the big moment. Yes, they are human, too, and may have anxiety, but they embrace the challenge. You, too, can use the antidote by being the hero of your own story.
  • Examine your values. The previous strategies fall under the umbrella of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). This moves deeper into existential matters of personal values and meaning. Most of us feel out of sorts when we are not aligned with our values. If your values include hard work, overcoming challenges, a job well done, etc., this is your chance. As Nelson Mandela once said, “I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it."
  • Finally, get used to uncertainty, ambiguity, and even a bit of chaos. Life is messy. Your brain will inevitably convince you that failure, disaster, and disappointment are around every corner. Unfortunately, it is occasionally right. However, with proper preparation, emotional regulation, and self-reflection, the result is almost always better than your mind would have you believe.

There is no need to fear the “poison” of your mind. It means well, and it is actually trying to help you survive. The antidote lies in being at peace with how your mind works and utilizing the ample strategies available to you that derive from that very same source.

item.title: The Fastest Way to Calm a Reactive Child
item.description:
Parenting

The Fastest Way to Calm a Reactive Child

Why changing a reactive child's behavior has almost nothing to do with the child.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Your child's brain reads your body before it processes your words.
  • Reactivity is not defiance wearing a louder costume. It's a stimulus-surge-behavior sequence.
  • A single differently-handled moment can change a pattern that's been running for months.

Sitting in my office, Janice recounted the following scene. It was 6:40pm on a Tuesday. She was feeling frustrated that dinner was getting cold. She repeated, seemingly gently, the same thing she said the prior Tuesday to her nine-year-old son, Ejijah, without incident. "Five more minutes, then we eat," but this time, Elijah erupted. Janice kept running the tape repeatedly back, until I gently stopped her. You see, she was looking for what she said was "wrong". But she was looking in the wrong place.

Focusing On The Tail End Blinds You To Where Reactivity Begins

After 35 years sitting across from families, I've come to think most of us watch the wrong end of the process. What you see when a child "loses it"—the yelling, the slammed door, the sudden stillness—is the tail end of a sequence: a small stimulus, an invisible surge inside a nervous system that just went offline, then the behavior, which is smoke after the fire's already burned. Stating your case in that window (e.g., "I already explained why," or "you know the rules") fails not because the child is stubborn, but because you're asking a brain with no current access to reasoning to reason with you.

Here's what I didn't fully appreciate until years into practice: your own nervous system is doing something just as automatic, and your child is reading it in real time. Long before kids can regulate themselves, they borrow regulation from the adults around them. As mental health professionals, we like to call this process co-regulation. A child's brain reads your facial tension and posture in a fraction of a second, well before it parses your sentence.

Your Child Keeps Your Body's Score

What this means is that you can say "I'm not upset" in an even voice while your jaw is tight and your shoulders are up by your ears, and your child's body will believe the jaw. I once worked with a mother convinced her three-year-old had "a hair-trigger," until we noticed his meltdowns started the instant her own body tightened a full breath before she'd said a word. He wasn't reacting to her sentence; he was reacting to her.

That's the premise behind my new book, 24 Hours to a Less Reactive Child. It explains how parents can lower their children's reactivity by being the thermostat rather than the thermometer. A thermometer reflects whatever heat or cold is already there; a thermostat holds a different temperature on purpose until the room comes around to it. To help your child lower their emotional reactivity, it is crucial for you to see yourself as the thermostat, not the thermometer. You'll likely be surprised by the downshift in your child's reactivity when you calmly set your own thermostat to the "calmer" setting.

The Research Behind Quick Resets That Bring High-Impact Change

Please hear that none of what I am writing here is just a clinical hunch. Decades ago, psychologist Moshe Talmon studied something that appeared to be a system failure: therapy clients who, for whatever reason, attended only a single session. He expected people who'd fallen through the cracks. Instead, he found many had gotten real, lasting benefit from that one hour of work, as he detailed in his book on "Single Session Therapy".

Walk-in clinics built on that premise have since spread through Australia, where Melbourne's Bouverie Center has studied single-session family therapy for years, with similar results: change often doesn't need months of accumulated insight. It needs one moment to land differently than it ever has before. And based on decades of my own clinical practice, I have seen many parents set the thermostat to a favorable level to quickly lower their children's reactivity.

The Takeaway

You can't rebuild your child's temperament by tomorrow. But you can change tonight's interaction—and that's usually the part that changes everything else.

item.title: The Ketamine Paradox
item.description:
Ketamine

The Ketamine Paradox

A breakthrough treatment meets an emerging public health challenge.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Ketamine can rapidly reduce severe depression, hopelessness, and suicidal thinking.
  • Repeated ketamine use can cause addiction, cognitive impairment, and potentially irreversible bladder damage.
  • The challenge is preserving ketamine’s therapeutic value while preventing misuse and reducing harm.

In the morning, a psychiatrist administers ketamine to help a suicidal patient rediscover hope. That evening, an emergency physician treats someone whose recreational ketamine use contributed to an accident, overdose, or dangerous drug combination. The same drug. Two very different stories. A treatment moves from the laboratory to carefully selected patients, and then, use expands. Then consequences emerge—not apparent or measurable—at the beginning.

The National Drug Early Warning System rang an alarm bell on July 17, 2026. NDEWS identified 71,924 nonfatal EMS encounters involving suspected ketamine overdoses nationwide between January 2023 and June 2026.

These data are alarming, but surveillance cannot establish illicit versus prescribed. Nevertheless, this is a public health signal that addiction medicine cannot ignore.

Ketamine's Two Stories
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

A New Way of Thinking About Depression

For 50+ years, ketamine has been an anesthetic in surgery, trauma care, and battlefield medicine. What changed was the question scientists asked. That question belonged to a Yale bench-to-bedside tradition I knew well. I worked with George Aghajanian, where LSD was studied not as a curiosity but as an instrument to gain insight into serotonin and the brain. George helped demonstrate that noradrenergic neurons become hyperactive during opioid withdrawal and that clonidine could suppress them. I helped carry those insights from rats into nonhuman primates and later human patients, establishing clonidine as the first non-opioid treatment for opioid withdrawal.

Ketamine grew from the Yale Psychiatry research culture that asked what an unusual drug might teach us about the brain. Decades later, Aghajanian’s research helped connect serotonin, glutamate, cortical plasticity, and rapid-acting antidepressant effects.

In 2000, John Krystal and his Yale colleagues reported that a subanesthetic ketamine dose could rapidly reduce major depression. Patients with treatment-resistant depression, hopelessness, or suicidal thinking sometimes improved within hours rather than weeks. Ketamine can save lives.

Ketamine also changed how we think about depression. Although it blocks NMDA receptors, no single receptor explains everything. It affects glutamate signaling, reward responsiveness, and cortical plasticity, perhaps loosening rigid brain activity and creating an opportunity for new learning.

A July 2026 Molecular Psychiatry study expands the story beyond glutamate. Investigators compared ketamine, its metabolite hydroxynorketamine, LSD, and psilocybin. Despite acting initially through different receptors, these rapid-acting antidepressants apparently converged on downstream neuroimmune pathways, particularly IL-7 and IL-15 signaling. Some biological signatures also distinguished ketamine responders from nonresponders.

These preliminary findings show why ketamine and psychedelics should be studied neither as miracle drugs nor solely as intoxicants. They may teach us how depression becomes entrenched—and reversed. That is also where ketamine treatment and ketamine addiction begin to intersect.

The Marketplace in Between

Racemic ketamine is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an anesthetic; psychiatric use is off-label. Esketamine (Spravato) nasal spray is approved for specific depressive disorders and administered under an FDA-regulated monitoring program. We once had two easily recognized categories: ketamine administered medically and ketamine obtained on the street. Now there is a third category between them. The home delivery market.

A 2026 study identified 233 clinics advertising ketamine treatment in metropolitan New York. More than one-third advertised at-home treatment, but only 51.5 percent listed a physician on the team.

At-home treatment is not automatically illegal or unsafe. Some programs provide appropriate evaluation, prescribing, monitoring, and follow-up; others provide far less. Uniform standards for patient selection, dosing, and duration are lacking.

In June 2026, the FDA warned 14 internet marketers who were selling unapproved or misbranded ketamine products. A package and mailing label are not substitutes for patient selection, standardized dosing, monitoring, and follow-up.

When Treatment Becomes Escape

In clubs and festivals, ketamine is used to produce dissociation, altered perception, and temporary escape. In an earlier Psychology Today post, I called this “Generation K.” Among New York City nightclub attendees, past-year use nearly doubled between 2017 and 2024, from 7.4 to 14.3 percent.

Nightclub populations do not represent all Americans, but often reveal emerging trends early. Every addictive drug becomes associated with something the person wants or needs. For some people, ketamine becomes associated with escape. Emotional distress → Ketamine → Rapid escape

The brain learns what it repeats. Tolerance increases. Doses escalate. More time is spent obtaining, using, and recovering from ketamine—attempts to cut down fail. Eventually, ketamine has become the brain’s learned solution to distress.

A Decade of New Medical Evidence

In 2016, my colleagues and I reviewed early evidence about ketamine misuse and diversion. We raised questions about addiction, cognition, and harm to the bladder and other organs. A decade later, we have more answers and medical complications.

Heavy ketamine use is also associated with cognitive impairment, persistent dissociative symptoms, severe abdominal pain known as “K-cramps,” and liver or biliary disease. One of the most devastating complications is ketamine-associated cystitis. It may begin with urinary frequency, urgency, pain, or bleeding, but repeated use can progressively shrink and scar the bladder.

Severe disease may lead to urinary obstruction, kidney damage, reconstructive surgery, or even bladder removal. Stopping ketamine early may permit substantial recovery. Once structural damage is advanced, however, some injury may be permanent.

Combining ketamine with other drugs adds another layer of danger.

A standard five-panel urine drug screen does not test for ketamine. If ketamine use is suspected, a urine test for ketamine and norketamine must be ordered. Blood testing may be useful in acute ketamine intoxication but has a shorter detection window.

There is no ketamine overdose antidote. Narcan is given when opioid contamination or co-use is possible.

Medical Ketamine Is Different

Carefully supervised ketamine treatment should never be confused with chronic, high-dose recreational use. Medical treatment includes patient selection, known composition and dosing, monitoring, follow-up, and a therapeutic goal. Nonmedical use may involve uncertain purity, escalating doses, dangerous combinations, craving, and dependence on dissociation to manage life.

We’ve learned this lesson before. Promising psychedelic research became entangled with recreational self-administration, weak science, counterculture advocacy, and Timothy Leary overwhelming scientific investigation, delaying research for decades.

The difference is not simply the setting or where ketamine is taken. It is why, how much, how often, under what safeguards, and what happens afterward. In medical treatment, the dose is determined and monitored by a clinician. With self-administration, the person may begin increasing the dose or frequency in pursuit of dissociation, relief, or an effect that no longer comes as easily. That loss of control is an early warning, the clearest sign that treatment may be turning into a ketamine use disorder.

The Better Question

During 50 years in addiction medicine, I have repeatedly watched valuable medications acquire a second identity. Morphine relieves pain. Benzodiazepines stop seizures. Stimulants improve attention. Each can also become a drug of misuse.

With ketamine, the question is not whether it’s good or bad. The better questions are: Who is the right patient? Under what supervision? For how long? With what safeguards? And toward what therapeutic goal?

Ketamine may prove to be one of psychiatry’s most important advances in decades. It is also becoming one of addiction medicine’s newest challenges. Our responsibility is to preserve its capacity to relieve depression, hopelessness, and suicidal suffering while preventing another generation from learning that dissociation is the only escape from emotional pain.

The brain learns what it repeats. Treatment must give it something better to learn.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Hidden Reason You Feel Empty Inside
item.description:
Emotions

The Hidden Reason You Feel Empty Inside

What that hollow feeling is really telling you and what to do about it.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Emptiness is one of the hardest feelings to name, so most people never link it to its real cause.
  • Feeling empty often traces back to childhood emotional neglect, when your feelings went unseen and unanswered.
  • You can fill the emptiness now by giving yourself the acceptance you did not get as a child.
Source: Tatyana Gladskih / StockAdobe

It's like I have no emotions. I'm numb a lot of the time.

Something is missing in me.

I have no idea how I feel about anything.

Sometimes my chest feels hollow.

I feel empty inside.

What looks like five unrelated statements is actually five different people describing the same feeling.

It's a hard emotion to identify, and even harder to put into words. Everyone says it differently because there is no standard label for it. But for these five people, and for thousands more, it is the same feeling, caused by the same problem.

The one word that captures it best:

Emptiness.

Of all the emotions you can have, “empty” may be one of the most uncomfortable, because to feel empty is to feel incomplete. It's the sense of something absent or missing inside you, of being different, set apart, alone, lacking, numb.

This is a feeling that can quietly drive you toward all sorts of unhealthy things: overeating, overdrinking, over-shopping, even using drugs. It erodes your joy, energy, and confidence, a little at a time. And it works in the dark. Emptiness flies under the radar, which is exactly what makes it so powerful.

What Emptiness Is Trying to Tell You

Every feeling you have carries a message about yourself, and “empty” is no different.

Empty tells you that something vital is missing inside you, something you need for happiness and fulfillment. Is it different for every person? I don't think so. From talking with scores of people who feel this way, I've come to believe what's missing is the same for everyone.

What's missing is emotion.

Childhood Emotional Neglect

Elena is 43, well-liked, good at her job, and married to a man she loves. From the outside, her life looks full. But most evenings, once the house goes quiet, she notices a hollow place in her chest she can't explain. "What is wrong with me?" she wonders. "I have everything I'm supposed to want. So why do I feel like I'm just going through the motions?"

Elena isn't ungrateful, and she isn't depressed, though she keeps expecting a doctor to tell her she is. What she feels is empty, and it traces back to a childhood she remembers as perfectly fine.

She has no idea that the actual cause of her discomfort is childhood emotional neglect.

Childhood emotional neglect happens when you grow up in a home where your emotions are not noticed, accepted, or responded to enough. It's not about what was done to you. It's about what didn't happen for you. And because it's made of absence rather than action, it leaves no mark you can point to.

It's important to say something here about Elena's parents, and very possibly about yours, too. They were not necessarily bad people. Most emotionally neglectful parents are doing their best, and many were emotionally neglected themselves as children. They simply could not give their children what no one had given them. This is why childhood emotional neglect is so often no one's fault.

Your emotions are hard-wired into you, the most deeply personal, biological part of who you are. When your parents fail to respond to your feelings, you automatically learn to do the same, without ever making a conscious choice. Walling off your emotions is not a decision but results from an invisible message with invisible power. As a child, you naturally adapt and wall off your own feelings; then you carry that habit straight into adulthood.

So when you feel empty now, what's missing is the very thing that was missing then: the acceptance and validation of your emotions. But here is the change that matters. In adulthood, you no longer need that acceptance from your parents. You only need it from yourself.

"But I Do Have Emotions"

Maybe you're saying that to me right now. "I do have feelings. So why do I still feel empty?"

Picture a wall inside you. On one side are your feelings. On the other side is you. Your emotions exist and are real, and now and then, one breaks through, and you feel it fully. But the wall is still there, and most of the time it holds your feelings just out of reach.

That wall is not a flaw. You built it as a child because you had to, and what you built, you can also begin to take down.

8 Signs That You Feel Emptiness

  1. At times, you feel physically empty inside.
  2. You are deeply uncomfortable with feeling, or appearing, needy.
  3. Sometimes you feel numb.
  4. You question the meaning and purpose of your life.
  5. For no obvious reason, you sometimes wonder what’s wrong with your life.
  6. You feel mystifyingly different from other people.
  7. Some important ingredient seems to be missing from your life.
  8. Deep down, you feel that you are alone.

What to Give Yourself Now

Here is the good news. The work is not to manufacture feelings you don't have. They are already in you, waiting on the other side of the wall, and all you have to do is let them through.

A few places to start:

  • Turn your attention inward. Several times a day, pause and ask yourself: What am I feeling right now? You may draw a blank at first. Ask anyway. That turn inward is the opposite of what you learned as a child.
  • Name what you find. When a feeling comes, put one word to it. Sad. Anxious. Relieved. Angry. Naming it is how you begin to know it.
  • Meet it with acceptance, not judgment. Don't call the feeling weakness or push it down. Your feelings are not a problem to solve. They are information about who you are and what you need.

This is the acceptance and validation you didn't get back then, offered to yourself now. Brick by brick, it's how the wall comes down.

You Can Fill the Emptiness

If this post describes you, please know this. Yes, something is missing. Yes, it is vital. But you are not needy, and you are not numb. You are not different, and you are not alone. Everything you need to fill yourself is already inside you, waiting for you to open your eyes, take down your wall, and see.

The fuel of life is feeling. If you weren't filled up in childhood, you can begin to fill yourself now. You were never meant to run on empty.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: Healing Is a Time-Release Capsule
item.description:
Resilience

Healing Is a Time-Release Capsule

Recovery is not linear. Self-compassion keeps its engine running.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Healing is rarely instant; like a time-release capsule, it can work gradually—even outside awareness.
  • Setbacks are part of recovery—and how you interpret them shapes what happens next.
  • Compassion from others creates the conditions for healing. Self-compassion keeps us able to use them.

We live in a world of instant everything. So when illness, trauma, grief, or heartbreak arrives, we quietly expect recovery to follow the same rules: Take the step, do the therapy, wake up fixed.

Healing rarely works that way. It behaves more like a time-release capsule: Change is delivered gradually, unevenly, and sometimes outside immediate awareness. And self-compassion, as we will see, does not perform all the work of healing—but it helps us remain engaged long enough for treatment, time, relationships, and repeated small choices to matter.

The Strange Mathematics of Suffering—and of Healing

Here is something three decades of clinical work have taught me: In the mathematics of suffering, 2 + 2 sometimes equals 10.

Pain does not always add up in simple increments; repeated wounds may sensitize people to later stress. The kindling hypothesis in recurrent depression proposes that, over time, increasingly modest stressors may become sufficient to trigger major episodes (Post, 1992). In lived experience, that can make 2 + 2 feel like 10—because the earlier suffering is still part of the current equation. A person devastated by a "small" setback is not being dramatic; the older sums are still on the page.

But healing can follow the same strange mathematics. Research on sudden gains in psychotherapy found that a substantial share of improvement often arrives not gradually but in jumps—large shifts between one session and the next, after long flat stretches (Tang & DeRubeis, 1999). Progress can remain hard to see and then become visible all at once; the earlier work was not wasted simply because its effects were not yet obvious. I have sat with people who, after years of struggle, turned a corner in a single week that no chart had predicted.

Why can small things become large? Because in ordinary arithmetic, small numbers stay small—but in human lives, they interact. Two modest injuries can activate a history of pain and feel like 10. Two modest acts of healing can restore sleep, or hope, or trust—and unlock changes far larger than either could produce alone.

Healing Is Not Linear

We picture recovery as a straight line pointing upward, each day a little better than the last. Anyone who has actually healed from anything knows it is a winding path: three steps forward, two back—some days five back—and some days spent sitting still, gathering strength.

Setbacks, in other words, are not a departure from healing; they are part of its route. Relapse research offers a finding worth memorizing. In relapse-prevention models for substance use, interpreting a lapse as total failure—"I've ruined everything"—can increase the risk of continued use, whereas treating it as information supports renewed coping (Witkiewitz & Marlatt, 2004). The wider lesson likely applies beyond addiction: A setback becomes most dangerous when it is converted into a global verdict about the self. The setback does not decide what happens next. Your interpretation of the setback does.

article continues after advertisement

The Gift of Compassionate Others

Along this path, other people matter enormously—the friend who listens without judgment, the family member who shows up on your worst day. A major meta-analysis found that people with stronger social relationships had a substantially greater likelihood of survival across the studies reviewed (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010); compassionate relationships are one important way those bonds become protective. Being surrounded by people who treat us with compassion is a gift beyond measure.

And yet it has a limit that took me years to understand: External compassion is not enough. You can be surrounded by the most loving people in the world and still speak to yourself with cruelty; you can be forgiven by others a thousand times and still refuse to forgive yourself. Compassion from outside is fuel, delivered faithfully to the door. Something inside has to burn it.

Self-Compassion: What Keeps Us in the Process

That something is self-compassion: treating yourself, in moments of failure and pain, with the kindness you would offer a dear friend—acknowledging the suffering without drowning in it, and remembering that imperfection is the human condition (Neff, 2003). A meta-analysis found that higher self-compassion is consistently associated with lower depression, anxiety, and stress (MacBeth & Gumley, 2012).

To be precise: Self-compassion is not the whole engine of healing. Recovery may also require effective treatment, safety, medication, rest, material support, and time. Self-compassion is what keeps us engaged with all of those when progress is slow, uneven, or painful. Listen to yourself on a bad day, and you can hear which voice is on duty. One says: "This is hard. I am doing my best. Setbacks are part of the process." The other says: "What is wrong with me? I should be further along by now." The first voice helps you stay in the process. The second makes every setback harder to survive.

The practice is unglamorous and daily. Notice the inner voice, and if you would not say those words to someone you love, try again—softer. Expect setbacks, so their arrival reads as part of the route rather than proof of failure. Measure progress in long intervals—this month against last year, not today against yesterday. Rest without guilt; rest is not withdrawal from healing but often part of the treatment. And count the small victories—the walk taken anyway, the hard conversation survived—because in healing's strange mathematics, small numbers interact.

article continues after advertisement

The Time-Release Promise

If you are in the middle of healing right now—from illness, grief, trauma, or whatever life has handed you—here is what the metaphor asks you to remember: The absence of visible progress today does not prove that no progress is occurring.

But patience is not passivity. If treatment is not helping, symptoms are worsening, or you are not safe, healing may require a different route—a different approach, clinician, or setting—not simply more waiting. A time-release capsule deserves time; the wrong prescription deserves a new conversation.

For the slow days and the invisible stretches, be patient with yourself, and speak gently to yourself, especially when it is hard. Self-compassion is not the reward you receive at the end of healing.

It is the engine that carries you there.

item.title: How Falsehoods Have Squeezed the Joy Out of Youth Athletics
item.description:
Sport and Competition

How Falsehoods Have Squeezed the Joy Out of Youth Athletics

Exploring the poisons infecting today's sports world for young people.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Sports is a word derived from "disport," meaning "to enjoy yourself, especially by doing physical activity.”
  • Youth sport as a business has undermined its purposes of youth athletics—to have fun and learn soft skills.
  • Poor adult conduct, including that of some coaches and parents, have injected venom into youth sports.

“To enjoy yourself, especially by doing physical activity.” That’s the Cambridge Dictionary definition of disport, a term seldom used that evolved into the more familiar word—sport.

Disport entered the English language between 1275 and 1325, deriving from the French word desport that translates to “amuse oneself in light or lively fashion."

That’s a reminder of what sports are intended for—physical activity that delivers fun and enjoyment--which was what the youth athletic experience is supposed to be about. Not so much anymore.

When properly conducted, athletics can also be an activity that trains “soft skills.” Competencies that enable work and social effectiveness, gained via constructive team process with coaches and fellow athletes. A few specific soft-skill examples include competent communication, goal setting, compassion, organization, and appropriate conduct, etc.

Forever life lessons.

All that has been undermined or completely obliterated by a current toxic youth sports culture, poisoned by involved adults, including parents and coaches. Those grown-ups have transformed a once rewarding pastime, infused with fun and life lessons galore, into an activity contaminated by threat, fear, falsehoods, and inappropriate conduct, producing more harm than good for youth participants.

There are a pair of virtuous organizations targeting these poisons to restore a positive youth sports experience that will be discussed in future posts. First, a review of the venomous ingredients that have contaminated today’s youth sports culture. Some have been discussed in these Sports Between the Ears posts: How Young Athletes Struggle for Identity Beyond Sports, How to Help Young Athletes Avoid a Narrow Sense of Self, and You're Far More Than an Athlete. We’ll briefly summarize a few of the bigger poisonous factors.

Youth Sport Entrepreneurs

Entrepreneurial coach spreading false expectations to young athletes.
Source: AI-generated photo by Gemini.

A leading contaminant of youth athletics is its conversion into a business pursuit. Fortune 500 wannabe coaches and sports program “executives” who have converted youth sports into a marketing, money chase.

Youth sports used to be affordable and community-based programming, serving local youth. Kids’ and community best interests were at the heart of those programs, not only teaching the skills required of a particular sport, but also the soft skills of lifelong value. Leadership, followership, coachability, discipline, being a virtuous teammate, sportsmanship, etc. It wasn’t about marketing or money.

The youth sports business model has forgotten about many of those valuable elements. Obscenely high, unaffordable fees of private business sports programs have prevented participation for many kids. Because so many young athletes have flocked to those sports’ biz teams and clubs, local community-based sports programs are floundering or shutting down due to dwindling participants.

Year-round demand for too much practice and specialization in one sport, as detailed here, are other sports joy killers. Kids feel forced by coaches and parents to engage in such physically and mentally demanding and exhausting expectations. Such a commitment can be fine if made by the athlete, not an overly zealous coach or parent.

Wildly unrealistic expectations and misrepresentations are other common poisoned ingredients of the youth sports business model.

Unrealistic Expectations and Falsehoods

Train and play for us, and you’ll earn a D1 college athletic scholarship. Given that less than 2% of high school athletes play Division 1 sports, according to NCAA data, that’s highly unlikely. Fewer than 7% of high school athletes go on to play DIII, DII, or DI college sports.

Despite all that, parents and youth buy into that sports biz marketing promise, believing that all the time and money poured into sports will pay off with a college athletic scholarship. It’s an understandable belief for kids, considering their youthful naivete. You’d think parents would know better. Nope!

When those college scholarships don’t materialize, frustration and sadness begin to creep in for many young athletes. Fear and desperation can take over. The threat that their unrealistic expectations are headed for the dumpster, and that all the time and money invested had failed to deliver. Now they have to face up to the embarrassment that ensues after having endless bragging on social media, and directly to friends, that they were going to play in college.

Enjoyment converted into dismay and dissatisfaction. Fear and threat have ruined their sports experience.

Sports programs advertising falsehoods, calling themselves “elite” and claiming their coaches are “experts,” titles mostly for marketing purposes with minimal to no factual basis. Yet, kids and parents buy right into it. No vetting of the claims of those programs or instructors, most of which are false.

Inappropriate Adult Conduct

Coaches and parents publicly ridiculing athletes and coaches of opposing teams during competitions and on social media. Some of those adults encourage their athletes to do the same, resulting in kids rage-baiting opposing athletes and teammates. More poison.

Screaming at their athletes when they make mistakes. A behavior that furthers the fear and pressure experienced by athletes in such circumstances, again diminishing enjoyment (and performance) for the sport. Competition is anxiety-provoking enough, without throwing in the threat of being publicly humiliated. Some coaches will angrily pull kids out of the game immediately after making a mistake. More fear and threat, further killing the joy.

The next two posts will take a look at two antidotes to combat sports toxicity.

Stay tuned.

item.title: Have You Forgiven Life?
item.description:
Grief

Have You Forgiven Life?

A way to get right with yourself.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • When life takes what is precious to us, it’s easy to remain angry, cynical, and distrustful.
  • Life is not fair, and it makes sense to stop pretending that it should be.
  • When we forgive life, we let go of being life’s victim.
Source: Amistad Cristiana / Unsplash

Most of us don’t think of the option of forgiving life. It might be easier to see that forgiving God is something we’re more comfortable considering. I prefer to focus on life as fashioned by the Creator. Life as the tendency to give and take. It can offer opportunities for love, belonging, achieving, joy, and satisfaction. Each of these can also be taken away as we experience a loss of love or isolation, sorrow, defeat, and disillusionment. Life can play the death card without any warning.

When We Don’t Forgive Life

There are a number of consequences when we either don’t see that forgiving life is a possibility, or we simply don’t want to do it.

  • Chronic anger: When life takes what is precious to us, it’s easy to remain angry. Intense anger acts as a wall distancing us from others. We may lose opportunities for love, friendship, collegiality, and collaboration.
  • Cynicism: It’s easy to remain cynical due to loss. Cynicism is a loss of faith in life, usually resulting in feeling lost and unable to discern what truly matters.
  • Remaining distrustful: Living with a compromised level of trust can happen when we experience loss because we were betrayed.
  • Being trapped in an analysis of fairness: Once we believe we have lived an upstanding life with no intent to harm anyone, we decide that what was taken from us is unfair. We can take up residency in the accusation that life is unfair. Of course, life is not fair, and it makes sense to stop pretending that it should be.
  • Risk avoidance: We can decide that we are able to control further losses by minimizing the risk we take. Such a decision actually has us living less.

Forgiving Life

Let’s look at how we can prepare to forgive life and what’s to be gained by doing so.

  • Life—not my life: We pave the way toward forgiving life when we can shed a bit of narcissism. It’s only too easy to see our losses as only about our lives as opposed to life itself. Life guarantees nothing, and your next breath is a gift.
  • Release from victimhood: When we forgive life, we let go of being life’s victim. It then becomes easier to be both grateful and generous.
  • Living on life’s terms: As we become more forgiving of life, we become more accepting of living life on life’s terms. Such acceptance entails the realization that life’s terms are so much larger than our intentions and plans.
  • Peace: Peace comes as we accept that life will give and life will take. We live with more gratitude for what is given and forgiveness for what is taken.
  • Courage: In the absence of fairness and predictability, being alive calls for courage. Courage means that we can face our fears, be clear about what we are asking of life, and be curious about what life asks of us.
  • A greater communal spirit: Forgiving life is typically accompanied by the recognition that offering help and getting help go a long way to generating more resiliency in the face of what life takes from us.

Forgiving life is not necessarily something that comes easily following a severe loss. We may need to grieve, which might include feeling betrayed by life. Let life know how betrayed you feel, how angry and disappointed you feel. Let your sorrow be heard by those who care for you. Being in the presence of your sorrow reminds others they are being touched by something so essentially human. It’s an invitation to their humanity. And as your sorrow story is witnessed with love and compassion, it makes its way into your narrative. You then carry a different sorrow story, one that has a profound kinship with forgiveness. It's you getting right with yourself.

item.title: People Are Messy. But You Can Work Well With Others Anyway.
item.description:
Career

People Are Messy. But You Can Work Well With Others Anyway.

We look for simple ways to understand others. But the mess might be the answer.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Every person's story is messy, including yours. Working together will always be a challenge.
  • AI advice about work relationships carries the bias the humans taught: the idea that each story is simple.
  • You can learn to accept the messy without understanding the whole story of every colleague.

Ask anyone the plot of Romeo & Juliet, and I'd bet you get a version of boy meets girl, boy and girl fall in love, warring families tear them apart and ultimately both end up dead. Ok, maybe you get: they make terrible decisions, relying on third parties in the pre-digital age to pass vital messages between them, because of their warring families. And end up dead.

But that isn't how we hold stories, so we reduce them to something easier to carry. And so does AI, probably because it reflects an even simpler version than humans can hold. I personally love AI, but all of us have seen it reduce things from complexity to simplicity, sometimes to laughable effect. But we do have to consider its teacher.

Source: Israel Andrade/Unsplash

As humans, we crave order. We see patterns and predictability, because we want to reduce risk. We learn that from an early age. The safe way home, the faster commute. It's deeply embedded in our survival instincts. Sometimes that requires overriding even rational signals. We trust people that we used to believe in longer than we should. We keep doing something that stopped working, because for so long it was the least risky move.

We're also incredibly self-interested. We suffer from confirmation bias. And as a result, we can be highly irrational. We're creating disorder while seeking it.

And the way humans simplify all that noise is to reduce the story to boy meets girl. No Rosaline (remember her?). No friar. No poor apothecary choices. Just a tale of star-crossed lovers destined to a fate beyond their control. It's a simple story. It's not Shakespeare's.

Working well with others requires accepting their messiness and ours

At work, that need to simplify the stories is in overdrive. We need to reduce threats as quickly as possible. We size up colleagues and bosses and power structures. The stories not only are simplified; they’re biased. We assume the people who manage us are more capable technically. Or, that they are good at office politics. Either story could be true. Probably both.

Working with others will never be easy because we all suffer from the same conflicting tendencies. Everyone is messy because everyone is looking for order, while sometimes acting irrationally to serve our own interests. If you can accept that, you will likely find it easier, not harder, to work with others. If you stop and assess someone's behavior as "is this the safe move for them?" it starts to make sense. You may not like it – but you'll understand it.

Don't fight the messiness. It's critical to the true story. Next, don't forget people are trying to make sense of you, too. They are simplifying your story as they scan you for risk. Other people don't know everything you are carrying. They don't know how their behavior lands. You don't know how yours does.

That does not indicate a failure as a human. But it's so much noise for a species that uses simplicity as a hard-wired survival tactic. And it works until it doesn't. It is right to be wary of a person who reminds us of someone who has injured us in the past. It is a sign of maturity to begin to tell the difference between who has our best interests at heart and who is merely performing it. We all need colleagues we can rely on, whose judgment we trust, whose commitment matches our own. The stories we tell ourselves are not bad or wrong. They are incomplete and biased. And who has time to learn everyone's life story?

But you don't have to learn everyone's story – all you have to remember is that you don't know all of it. Nor they, yours. And as we all use AI more to help navigate work situations – don't forget your ill-formed understanding of all this messiness is distilled down to however much you tell AI, who further reduces it to a story that serves your self-interest.

What could possibly go wrong?

Work relationships are more fragile by nature. Because work relationships are largely unchosen, and are high stakes, we are even more likely to shorthand the stories. Our experiences with colleagues are more one-dimensional. We "just" work together. We keep personal information more limited and sanitized. Friends and family are stronger relationships because they are forged tighter by sharing times of adversity and vulnerability.

Colleagues exist to help us enrich ourselves. And a negative outcome that we perceive as the fault of someone we have a transactional relationship with lands hard. You mess up, I'm worried about my job security (or bonus, or promotion). This fragile relationship impacts our ability to support ourselves – and our friends and family, which are the stronger relationships to begin with. Put simply, we trust colleagues less, because we care about other relationships more.

Working well with others is an ongoing process, not a to-do list

We are not problems to be solved but paradoxes to be lived with. You aren't going to change the messiness. The term "organization" isn't accidental – it's a bunch of messiness assembled to be more productive than each of us can produce alone. That doesn't mean work relationships are doomed to fail. Or that they remain transactional: I have amazing, authentic friendships with people that I stopped working with years ago. The point is those relationships that fatigue you at work can't go away. They will likely exist everywhere you work. The skill to learn is to accept the whole messy, unknowable story. The one in your head, and the one in theirs. You don't have to know all of it – any more than you need to recite Shakespeare. You just have to remember the whole thing is a lot messier than the summary.

item.title: AI Can Predict; Entrepreneurs Still Have to Judge
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Can Predict; Entrepreneurs Still Have to Judge

AI maps the patterns, but founders decide which unproven futures survive.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Entrepreneurial judgment is the ability to make and own decisions when outcomes cannot be reliably predicted.
  • AI improves the breadth and depth of analysis, but also reduces originality and creates misplaced confidence.
  • The strongest decisions combine AI assistance with expertise, experimentation, and human accountability.

This post is co-authored by Dr. Tony Nguyen and Dr. Giang Hoang.

In an age of instant analysis, the most valuable entrepreneurial skill may be knowing when no reliable answer exists.

Imagine two entrepreneurs considering the same business idea. Both ask an artificial intelligence (AI) tool to identify customers, analyze competitors, recommend a price, forecast demand, and produce a launch plan. Within minutes, each receives an impressively detailed response.

The first entrepreneur treats the output as an answer. The second treats it as a collection of assumptions. That difference is entrepreneurial judgment.

As generative AI becomes embedded in entrepreneurship, founders can access more information, generate more alternatives, and complete analytical work faster than ever. But having more analysis is not the same as knowing what to do. In fact, when polished answers are available instantly, the psychological ability to question, interpret, and act on those answers may become one of the entrepreneur's most important advantages.

What Is Entrepreneurial Judgment?

Entrepreneurial judgment is often described as decision-making under uncertainty. But this definition needs some unpacking.

Some decisions involve risk. The possible outcomes are known, and their probabilities can at least be estimated. An established retailer deciding how much inventory to order can examine previous sales, seasonal patterns, and customer demand. The calculation may be imperfect, but useful historical evidence exists.

Entrepreneurs frequently face something more difficult: genuine uncertainty. Under uncertainty, the entrepreneur may not know all the possible outcomes, much less their probabilities. Customers may not understand a product that does not yet exist. A new technology may change how people behave. Competitors may respond unpredictably. Regulations, social expectations, and market categories may evolve as the venture develops.

There is no formula that can reliably determine whether people will adopt a radically new product, whether an unfamiliar business model will become legitimate, or whether a founder can persuade others to support a vision they cannot yet fully see. Judgment begins where the dependable decision rule ends.

Recent entrepreneurial judgment theory connects judgment with intention. Entrepreneurs do not merely observe possible futures; they decide which future is worth pursuing and begin directing their attention, effort, and resources toward it. Judgment therefore involves several psychological acts:

  • Imagining a possible future.
  • Developing a belief about what could create value.
  • Choosing among competing interpretations.
  • Committing resources before the outcome is known.
  • Revising the original belief as reality responds.
  • Accepting responsibility for the consequences.

Judgment is not simply intuition, confidence, intelligence, or decisiveness. A person can be highly confident and exercise poor judgment. Someone can possess extensive data but misunderstand what it means. Good judgment combines knowledge, imagination, interpretation, self-awareness, and the willingness to act without the comfort of certainty.

AI Makes Answers Easier—But Not Necessarily Better

AI is particularly effective when a problem contains recognizable patterns, abundant data, and relatively stable objectives. It can compare options, summarize evidence, uncover correlations, identify inconsistencies, and generate scenarios at a speed no unaided entrepreneur can match. This can make entrepreneurs more capable.

In a controlled experiment involving 124 entrepreneurs, Matteo Cristofaro and his colleagues found that AI assistance increased the number of opportunities participants recognized. It also improved the depth of their assessments, exploitation plans, and contextual analysis.

However, the study found an important trade-off: AI use also reduced novelty in opportunity recognition and innovation in proposed exploitation strategies.

The strongest performance came from entrepreneurs who combined AI with substantial sector knowledge. Their expertise allowed them to benefit from structured analysis without simply accepting it. They could recognize when an output was useful, when it lacked context, and when experience suggested an unconventional alternative. Without sufficient knowledge, an entrepreneur may be unable to distinguish a genuinely insightful AI recommendation from one that is merely fluent, generic, or inappropriate.

AI Changes the Psychology of Confidence

Generative AI does not merely provide information; it produces information in a persuasive form. Its answers are organized, articulate, and often delivered without visible hesitation. This fluency can create a psychological illusion: Because an explanation sounds coherent, it feels well-founded. Yet plausibility is not the same as truth.

AI can produce two opposite errors:

  1. False confidence: It can make a weak idea appear more convincing than the available evidence justifies, building a venture on questionable assumptions.
  2. Undue skepticism: It can make a truly original idea appear less credible because little historical precedent exists for it.

Researchers Farsan Madjdi and Bernd Wurth describe this as an AI-mediated plausibility regime. When AI systems influence funding, accelerator admissions, or platform visibility, they help determine which entrepreneurial futures appear reasonable. This matters because many transformative ideas initially look unreasonable. If investors, organizations, and founders increasingly rely on the same historical data and similar AI systems, unconventional ideas may be filtered out before they can prove themselves.

The Danger of Entrepreneurial Sameness

While AI helps an individual entrepreneur produce more ideas, widespread reliance on similar tools at the ecosystem level may produce greater conformity.

Richard Hunt and Rasim Serdar Kurdoglu call this potential effect algorithmic deforestation. Entrepreneurial ecosystems resemble rainforests; they depend on diversity, experimentation, unusual combinations, failed attempts, and unexpected discoveries. Because AI systems are designed to identify patterns and reduce undesirable variation, thousands of entrepreneurs using similar models may gradually converge on similar answers. Each entrepreneur becomes more efficient while the ecosystem becomes less diverse.

Entrepreneurial judgment protects the unusual observation, the local insight, the personal conviction, and the seemingly irrational experiment that a predictive model may dismiss as noise.

Judgment Is Not the Rejection of AI

The answer is not to avoid AI or romanticize unaided human intuition, which remains vulnerable to overconfidence, confirmation bias, and sunk-cost fallacies. AI can help expose these weaknesses by challenging assumptions and examining alternative scenarios.

The healthiest relationship is dialogue, not delegation. Entrepreneurs can strengthen judgment by:

  • Separating prediction from judgment: Use AI for repeatable, data-rich patterns, and rely on human judgment for unprecedented situations.
  • Asking AI to create disagreement: Prompt the tool to generate competing interpretations and challenge the founder's assumptions.
  • Protecting firsthand knowledge: Maintain direct contact with customers, observations, and operational experience.
  • Running small experiments: Use prototypes, pilot programs, and pre-orders to transform uncertainty into evidence.
  • Keeping accountability human: Retain personal responsibility for financial losses, team communication, and ethical consequences.

The Skill That Becomes More Visible

A polished pitch or a convincing strategy can be generated in minutes. What remains difficult is deciding which assumptions deserve belief, which possibilities are worth pursuing, when the evidence is sufficient to act, and when an apparently sensible recommendation should be ignored.

These are judgments, not calculations. The entrepreneurs who thrive in the age of AI will not be those who receive the best answers from a machine, but those who understand which questions remain theirs to answer.

item.title: Still Waiting for Your Parent to Change?
item.description:
Attachment

Still Waiting for Your Parent to Change?

Understanding the psychology of hope, attachment, and acceptance.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • The hope that endured in childhood can become a source of suffering in adulthood.
  • Acceptance means seeing your parent clearly and realistically.
  • Grieving the parent you wished you had creates space for healthier boundaries and greater peace.
Source: Felipe Moutinho/Pexels

"I know my parent probably isn't going to change…but maybe this time will be different."

I've heard countless versions of this statement in my psychotherapy practice. Sometimes it's spoken after a painful holiday gathering. Other times it follows another critical phone call or interaction in which an adult child once again feels unseen, criticized, dismissed, or emotionally wounded.

Intellectually, many adult children recognize that their parent is unlikely to become the nurturing, emotionally available, validating person they have longed for. Emotionally, however, letting go of that hope can feel almost impossible.

There is a good reason for this. During childhood, hope wasn't simply a wish—it was often a psychological necessity.

Hope Helps Children Survive

Children are biologically wired to seek closeness with their caregivers. Attachment theory tells us that children depend on their parents not only for physical survival but also for emotional regulation, safety, and the development of their sense of self (Bowlby, 1988). Unlike adults, children cannot realistically conclude, "My parent(s) aren’t emotionally capable of meeting my needs, so I'll stop expecting it."

Instead, they often arrive at another explanation: If I'm better—more successful, more lovable, less difficult—then maybe they'll finally notice me, approve of me, or love me the way I need.

This belief protects children from an unbearable reality. Accepting that the very people they depend on may never consistently provide emotional safety is far more threatening than believing change is still possible.

From a developmental perspective, this adaptation is remarkably intelligent. Hope preserves attachment and promotes survival. The challenge is that what protects us during childhood can quietly imprison us in adulthood.

When Childhood Hope Becomes Adult Pain

Many adults continue approaching their parents with the same emotional blueprint they developed decades earlier. They hope this holiday will be different, this accomplishment will finally earn approval, or this conversation will finally bring understanding.

When those hopes are disappointed, the pain extends far beyond the present moment. Feelings of rejection, shame, sadness, or inadequacy often reflect not only today's interaction but years of unmet emotional needs resurfacing.

In many ways, the nervous system is faithfully following a childhood survival strategy that once made perfect sense.

When Hope Keeps Us Stuck

Hope itself is not the problem. Healthy hope fosters resilience, perseverance, and healing. False hope is different. It repeatedly asks us to invest emotional energy in outcomes that remain outside our control. It suggests, "Maybe if I explain myself one more time, they'll finally understand." Meanwhile, years pass.

Adult children may tolerate criticism they would never accept from others, repeatedly overlook emotional abuse, struggle to establish boundaries, or spend days emotionally recovering from interactions that replay familiar patterns.

The suffering often comes not only from what happened today, but from today's disappointment colliding with yesterday's hope.

Grieving Someone Who Is Still Alive

One reason acceptance feels so difficult is that it often involves ambiguous loss, a concept developed by Pauline Boss (2021). Ambiguous loss occurs when someone is physically present but emotionally unavailable.

Unlike death, there is no clear ending. Your parent is still alive. You may still celebrate holidays together or talk every week. Yet the emotionally nurturing parent you longed for may never exist.

Every interaction can rekindle hope while simultaneously reminding you of what has always been missing. Because there is no definitive ending, the grief often remains unresolved. The mind naturally continues searching for a different outcome, making it difficult to stop hoping even when decades of experience suggest otherwise.

Many adult children return repeatedly hoping for a different ending to a story that has rarely changed. What they are grieving isn't simply a difficult parent; they are grieving the relationship they always believed was still possible.

This grief is often compounded by disenfranchised grief, a term introduced by Kenneth Doka (2022). Unlike bereavement following death, this loss is rarely acknowledged. There is no funeral, no ritual, and often little validation.

Instead, people hear comments like, "She's still your mother," or "He did the best he could." Although often well-intentioned, these responses can unintentionally minimize a profound emotional loss. Healing often begins when we recognize that we aren't grieving the loss of a parent, we're grieving the loss of the parent we needed.

Acceptance Is Not Giving Up

Many people fear that acceptance means approving of their parent's behavior or abandoning hope altogether. It doesn't. Acceptance means acknowledging reality as it is rather than continually negotiating with it in hopes that it becomes something different.

It says, "This is who my parent has consistently shown themselves to be." That clarity allows us to respond thoughtfully instead of reacting from the familiar cycle of hope followed by disappointment.

Paradoxically, acceptance often increases compassion—not because our parents suddenly deserve different treatment, but because we stop expecting them to become someone they have never demonstrated they can be.

Perhaps the most important distinction is this: False hope says, "Maybe they'll finally become the parent I need." Healthy hope says, "Even if they never change, I am worthy and whole and can still heal."

Healthy hope redirects our energy away from changing another person and toward building the life we want. It reminds us that we can learn healthier boundaries, cultivate emotionally safe relationships, and become the nurturing adult our younger self desperately needed.

What Healing Looks Like

Healing often begins with grief, not grieving the loss of your parent, but grieving the loss of the parent you deserved. Although painful, grief serves an important psychological purpose. It helps you stop investing emotional energy in changing the past and begin investing in your future.

Several practices can support this process:

First, notice when hope quietly becomes expectation. Before seeing your parent, ask yourself, "Am I expecting them to respond differently than they consistently have?" If so, gently return to what history, not wishful thinking has shown you.

Second, practice radical acceptance, a core principle of Dialectical Behavior Therapy (Linehan, 2015). Radical acceptance means recognizing that fighting reality often prolongs suffering, while accepting it gives you sovereignty, and allows you to choose your response.

Third, establish boundaries that protect your emotional well-being rather than trying to change your parent's behavior. Boundaries might include shortening visits, avoiding emotionally charged topics, declining abusive conversations, or recognizing when greater emotional distance is healthier than repeated emotional injury.

Fourth, intentionally cultivate emotionally healthy relationships. Research suggests that supportive relationships can foster what attachment researchers call earned secure attachment, allowing people to develop healthier relational patterns despite adverse childhood experiences (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2019; Siegel, 2020).

Finally, offer yourself the compassion you spent years hoping to receive from someone else. Kristin Neff's research demonstrates that self-compassion promotes emotional resilience, healthier coping, and greater psychological well-being (Neff, 2015).

The paradox is that acceptance doesn't make you love your parent less. It simply asks you to love reality more than fantasy. When you stop measuring every interaction against the relationship you wished you had, you become less emotionally captive to disappointment and more grounded in what is.

The child inside you needed hope to survive. The adult inside you needs acceptance to heal. Healing doesn't require your parent to become someone different. It begins when your emotional well-being and sense of wholeness and worthiness no longer depends on whether they do.

True freedom comes from becoming that source of love, protection, and compassion for yourself, because you were and are always deserving.

To reinforce healing, listen to a Loving Kindness Guided Meditation led by me.
