item.title: 4 Signs That You’re a Truly Grateful Person
item.description:
Gratitude

4 Signs That You’re a Truly Grateful Person

Unpacking the "4Gs" of grateful stories.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Personal narratives offer a deep look at how gratitude functions in everyday life.
  • Grateful stories are marked by four themes: gifts, grace, givers, and generosity.
  • Intentionally weaving the four Gs into the stories you tell can help cultivate gratitude.

How do you tell if you’re a truly grateful person?

To study individual differences in gratitude, researchers typically use self-report rating scales, of which the best-known is the six-item Gratitude Questionnaire, or GQ-6. Participants rate statements on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Responses are then summed, with higher scores indicating higher levels of gratitude.

I admire the GQ-6’s elegance and brevity and have used it in my own research. But it may have difficulty distinguishing among people at the grateful end of the spectrum. Across several studies, participants have reported scores clustered near the top of the scale. In one study of U.S. professionals, the average GQ-6 score was 38.50, within a theoretical range of 6 to 42. That’s an average response of about 6.4 on a 7-point scale.

Maybe many people really are very grateful. But high scores could also reflect people’s tendency to engage in socially desirable responding when completing the GQ-6. That is, many people think of gratitude as a desirable trait to have, and previous research has shown that their responses to the GQ-6 partially reflect their attempt to describe themselves in especially favorable terms.

This doesn’t mean the GQ-6 is invalid. But questionnaires may not tell the whole story.

The Stories You Tell Yourself and Others

If I want a richer picture of how gratitude operates in your life, I’d invite you to tell me stories about your life. I wouldn’t necessarily ask for a story that demonstrates gratitude. Instead, I might ask you to describe a memorable incident from the past week, the past year, or your childhood. Who was involved? When and where did it happen? Why is the event memorable?

Researchers call this the narrative approach. I like it because I believe human beings are inherently storytellers—we tell ourselves stories to make sense of our lives and we tell others stories about our lives to explain how we became the person we are. And you can learn a lot about yourself from the stories you tell.

Big, Middle, and Mini Stories

This is the second post in a mini-series on the narrative approach to understanding gratitude. In the first post, I introduced the life story: the overarching narrative through which people explain how they became who they are. You might call it the big story of your life. I argued that grateful people understand themselves as both receivers and givers of goodness.

But the big story is built from smaller ones, namely, mini stories and middle stories, which are the focus of this post.

Mini stories describe discrete episodes lasting from a few minutes to a day: lunch with a friend, a visit to the zoo, or receiving important medical news.

Middle stories describe broader periods of life, such as high school, recovering from an illness, or childhood summers with grandparents.

The 4Gs of Grateful Stories

Stories are not unfiltered windows into the self. There’s an editorial element in storytelling. To understand how gratitude appears in mini and middle stories, I’d pay attention not only to what happened but also to how the narrator makes sense of them. How does the narrator explain what caused the events in these stories and what they reveal about themselves or others?

But I wouldn’t simply count how often someone uses the words “grateful” or “gratitude.” Those words can be used habitually or performatively. Instead, I would look for recurring patterns of grateful interpretation.

I suspect the following four themes are likely to appear in grateful stories: gifts, grace, givers, and generosity.

1. Gifts

Grateful people tell stories about benefits they did not create or fully earn.

These gifts may come from other people, circumstances, nature, or chance. They might include a friend’s encouragement, an unexpected opportunity, good weather, or beautiful scenery.

In their stories, grateful people’s attention is drawn not only to what went wrong but also to the goodness that entered their lives.

2. Grace

Grateful people notice moments when kindness, patience, forgiveness, or opportunity exceeded what they think they were entitled to. I call this the abundance mindset and it shows up in their stories.

For example, they might mention a moment where they screwed up badly but, to their surprise, their supervisor or spouse responded with kindness rather than judgment.

3. Givers

Grateful people notice not only the gifts they receive but also the people who provide them.

In their stories, they name the teachers, relatives, friends, colleagues, neighbors, and strangers who contributed to their happiness or success.

4. Generosity

Grateful narrators often attend to the goodwill behind another person’s actions toward them. They infer a motive of generosity in their actions. In turn, grateful people tend to be generous to others as a means of paying it forward. These experiences of generosity show up regularly in their stories.

So, Are You Grateful?

No single story can establish whether someone is a grateful person. But recurring patterns across many stories may reveal habits of grateful interpretation.

If you keep a journal, read through what you have written. Notice how you describe the events of your life. If you have a spouse, partner, or close friend, ask what kinds of stories they hear you tell most often.

Do the 4Gs appear? Do your mini and middle stories contain gifts you did not create, moments of unexpected grace, givers who enriched your life, and experiences of generosity?

And just as our stories reveal our gratitude—or lack of it—so too can they be used as a tool to help us cultivate gratitude. Here’s a simple recommendation: if you want to be grateful, find ways to incorporate the 4Gs into the stories you tell yourself and others.

Suppose you’re walking home one evening and pause to notice a beautiful sunset. That’s a mini story from your life. You might think, “Wow, the sunset is beautiful!”

But you could go further to recognize it as a gift: something you did not create, cannot possess, and were fortunate to witness. You could further reflect on how precious this experience is. You recognize that not everyone has access to it. After all, there are people who work indoors during sunset who don’t get to witness it.

These small acts of interpretation turn an ordinary event into a grateful story.

Let the 4Gs become an integral part of the stories you tell yourself and others. But don’t just notice these grateful stories. Write them down. Recount them. Tell them to others.

Because, in the end, you become the stories you tell.

If this post resonated with you, you might also enjoy my Substack newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

item.title: Endurance Is a Team Sport
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Endurance Is a Team Sport

How our big challenges matter to each other.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • You will want to quit. More than once.
  • Support is not optional for big commitments.
  • Your journey matters to others and their journeys matter to you.

At some point in the night, every long ultra race stops being about strength and becomes a conversation between your body and your will. And if you stay out there long enough, something else enters the conversation too: the undeniable realization that you cannot do this alone.

Back in March, I participated in the Badger Mountain Challenge—a 50-mile race that turned out to be the single hardest race I’ve ever done.

I pinned bib number 399 to the left leg of my running tights in the early morning hours, stood at the start line with that singular combination of excitement and terror that comes with big commitments, and tried to go through my list in my head one more time. Headlamp? Yep. Extra battery pack for my phone? Uh huh! Food and liquid to keep me going between aid stations? Got it. Toilet paper for a full bladder between aid stations. In my pocket. I was ready.

But 50 miles isn't just a distance—it’s a decision. One that you have to keep making, step after step, long after the initial adrenaline fades (which is in about 20 minutes if your first mile is straight up a mountain trail).

The early miles were hard but manageable. Even beautiful. There’s a beat you fall into in an endurance event. That rhythm of your feet is what you lean into when it dawns on you that hours from now, when everyone in your life is counting sheep, you’ll be step, step, stepping up another mountain trail. Just get into the groove!

Source: Tanya Paquet/Unsplash

By the time I was climbing the long, exposed hills later in the day, the sun was relentless. My legs were heavy. Every incline felt personal, as though the mountain itself had something to prove. I grew tired, naturally, but I just cranked up the music in my earbuds and kept my eyes on the ground so I wouldn’t bite it in the loose gravel.

On and on I went.

And then, after I’d been out on the trail for 12 hours, I started to hear the voices that tempt you to do what is easiest instead of what you’ve committed to do.

You’ve gone far enough.
This is good.

People will still think you’re amazing, even if you don’t finish.
No one would blame you for calling it off here.

By nightfall, I felt like quitting was actually the reasonable thing to do. The course became harder to follow the further into the night I went. At mile 35 I even asked the volunteers at the aid station if someone could take me back to the finish line, but they told me they weren't a rescue station. I would have to get five miles further up the road to the mile 40 station.

My body was so depleted. I wasn’t running so much as moving forward in stubborn increments. That’s when the isolation set in—the kind that goes beyond being physically alone and makes everything feel more fragile.

Just as I was about to sit down and cry between aid stations, my phone buzzed.

A text from my brother. “B*tch, you can’t quit. Not today. Tomorrow. But not today.” It was 11:42 p.m.

I replied to him, speaking into Siri, “Tomorrow is in 20 minutes. Can I quit then?”

“No, dumb@ss. Then it will be today again.”

I had to laugh. Only a younger sibling could get away with talking to me like this.

Then another text came in—from two of his kids. I’d shared my location with them and they’d apparently started tracking me. Middle of the night and my grown niece and nephew were cheering me on. Sending messages into the dark: “You’re killing it!”

The cheering helped, but I was in so much pain. I just didn’t know if I could keep going. Still… I did.

Until the unthinkable happened. More than 20 hours into the race, I got lost.

Completely off course. No markers. No other runners. Just me, in the dark, trying to make sense of where I had gone wrong. Fatigue does strange things to your brain. It shrinks your problem-solving skills to the size of pea. Peabrain. A lost ultra-runner must have coined that phrase.

I stood in the middle of the trail, dumbfounded, for a full five minutes, feeling the edge of panic creep in. I sat down on the dirt and let a tear trickle down my dirty face. I decided I was going to quit the damn race, wait until daylight, find a spot in the nearest town on my GPS to hike to, and take a Lyft back to my hotel.

And then my phone buzzed again. It was my nephew, 34 years old, my nephew is fighting advanced cancer. He was still up watching me at two in the morning. The text read simply, “YOU ARE NOT GOING TO QUIT.” I don’t know if he tracked that I wasn’t moving or if he just had the urge to text.

Suddenly, I understood something. My race wasn't just mine. It belonged to the people who were cheering me on, too. And my nephew, running in a race he didn't sign up for and couldn't quit at will, was telling me he needed me to push.

I stood up and I did something crazy. I asked for help. I called my friend who was waiting for me at the finish line who got hold of the race director for me.

He picked up. I heard his voice on the phone sounding calm and grounded as he talked me through where I was. Helped me retrace my steps and guided me back toward the finish line.

I crossed the finish line in 22 hours and 32 minutes (having put in three extra miles due to being lost).

But here’s the truth: that finish didn’t belong to me alone.

It belonged to my brother and his kids, who stayed connected to me through the long night. It belonged to my friend who was on the other end of my frantic call. It belonged to the race director, who was my rock on the phone when I needed direction. It belonged to every moment I allowed myself to receive support instead of pretending I didn’t need it.

We tend to tell stories of endurance as personal victories. Grit. Determination. Inner strength. But that’s not the whole story, is it?

If you’re in the middle of something big—writing a book, building a business, rebuilding your life—here are a few things worth holding onto:

1. You will want to quit. More than once.
That doesn’t mean you’re failing. It means you’re in it. Expect the doubt. Plan for it. Wanting to call it off is just part of the deal in the middle of the proverbial night.

2. Support is not optional for big commitments.
You can resist it. You can try to go it alone. But at some point—usually when it matters most—you’re gonna need someone to remind you who you are and where you’re going. Lean in!

3. Your journey matters to others and their journeys matter to you. We are watching each other navigate this life. “If he can do it, I can do it,” You might think. And if you can do it—hard as it is, there might be someone in your life who will find the courage they need for their own hard thing.

Endurance isn’t just about staying the course. It’s about staying connected to yourself and others while you navigate the trail.

No one crosses the finish line for a long race alone. If you’re in a hard place right now, reach out to your cheerleaders. You’ll be able to return the favor someday for sure.
